title: Virtual Nodes
description: Solve the uneven distribution problem with virtual nodes, and learn how to handle heterogeneous hardware in a consistent hashing ring.

segments.text: Last lesson we built the hash ring and saw its elegance. But we ended with a problem: with only a few physical servers, the ring can be wildly unbalanced. One server might handle six times more data than another. Let's fix that.

Look at this ring with three servers. Server A owns this massive arc, server B has a tiny slice, and server C is somewhere in between. This isn't just unfair — it's dangerous. Server A will become a hotspot and eventually a bottleneck.

Here's the key insight: what if each physical server appeared at multiple positions on the ring? Instead of one point per server, we place dozens or even hundreds of points. Each of these points is called a virtual node.

Server A gets virtual nodes A-zero, A-one, A-two, and so on. We hash each virtual node name to place it on the ring. Now server A has many small arcs spread around the ring instead of one big unpredictable arc.

With enough virtual nodes, the law of large numbers kicks in. The total arc owned by each server converges toward one-Nth of the ring. In practice, 100 to 200 virtual nodes per server gives you a very even distribution.
segments.thought_prompt: Why do you think we need 100+ virtual nodes and not just 5 or 10?

segments.text: Virtual nodes solve another problem beautifully. What if your servers have different capacities? A beefy 64-core machine should handle more data than a tiny 4-core instance. With virtual nodes, you simply assign more virtual nodes to more powerful servers.
Give the big server 300 virtual nodes and the small server 50. The big server will naturally own about six times more of the ring. Load distribution now matches hardware capacity, automatically.

When you add a new server, you add its virtual nodes one by one. Each virtual node steals a tiny slice from a different existing server. The data migration is spread across all existing servers instead of burdening just one neighbor.

The trade-off? More virtual nodes means more metadata to store and more entries in the routing table. But this is a tiny amount of memory compared to the data being distributed. It's almost always worth it.
segments.thought_prompt: What would happen if you used a million virtual nodes per server? Is more always better?

segments.text: Cassandra uses 256 virtual nodes per server by default. DynamoDB uses a similar approach. Even Amazon's original Dynamo paper from 2007 extensively discusses virtual nodes as essential for production-grade consistent hashing.

Virtual nodes transform consistent hashing from a clever idea into a production-ready system. Even distribution, heterogeneous hardware support, and smooth scaling. That's the complete consistent hashing story: the ring gives you minimal data movement, and virtual nodes give you balanced load.
